title: Special Use Airspace — Prohibited, Restricted, Warning, MOA, Alert, and TFRs

questions.text: A VFR pilot's route passes directly through an active Military Operation Area (MOA) labeled 'Eglin 1 MOA' on the sectional chart. The pilot has not contacted the controlling authority and does not have an ATC clearance. Is the pilot legally permitted to transit the MOA under 14 CFR 91.133?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — but only during weekday hours between 0800 and 1700 local; MOAs are automatically inactive outside of published training hours, eliminating any legal or practical restriction on civilian entry

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — VFR aircraft may operate in an MOA without ATC authorization or prior coordination; MOAs designate areas of military activity but do not legally restrict civilian VFR entry; the pilot should exercise extreme caution and be alert for military aircraft

options.label: C
options.text: No — VFR flight through an MOA during any activity requires flight at or above 18,000 MSL to remain clear of low-level military operations; VFR below 18,000 through an active MOA violates Class A airspace restrictions that automatically apply to active MOAs

options.label: D
options.text: No — MOAs have the same entry requirements as Restricted Areas; ATC clearance from the controlling military authority is required before entering any active MOA for VFR or IFR aircraft; failure to obtain authorization violates 14 CFR 91.133

questions.explanation: Military Operation Areas (MOAs) do NOT legally prohibit VFR aircraft entry. 14 CFR 91.133 prohibits civil aircraft from operating in Prohibited Areas and Restricted Areas without authorization — but MOAs are not Restricted Areas. VFR pilots may legally enter and transit an active MOA without ATC authorization or prior clearance. This is a critical legal distinction that the DPE tests. However, legal entry does not mean safe entry: active MOAs contain military aircraft performing aerobatics, high-speed low-altitude maneuvers, and supersonic operations. The practical recommendation is to check the MOA's activity status before transiting and to remain vigilant for military traffic. IFR aircraft DO need ATC coordination to transit an active MOA (ATC will not route IFR through an active MOA without military coordination). The 'MOA equals a Restricted Area' answer incorrectly equates MOA entry rules with Restricted Area rules. The 'weekday hours only' answer invents an automatic inactive schedule — MOA activation schedules vary and must be confirmed in real time. The 'Class A overlay' answer invents a Class A overlay for active MOAs.

questions.text: A pilot checks the sectional chart for a cross-country and sees no Prohibited Areas, Restricted Areas, or other SUA restrictions along the planned route. The pilot does not check NOTAMs. Upon departure, the pilot inadvertently penetrates an active Presidential TFR published 45 minutes prior to the flight. What is the regulatory nature of this violation?

options.label: A
options.text: Violation of 14 CFR 91.141 and 14 CFR 91.103 — Presidential TFRs are published as NOTAMs only (sectional charts are published every 6 months and cannot depict real-time TFRs); the pilot's failure to obtain a NOTAM briefing was a violation of the preflight action requirement of 14 CFR 91.103; ignorance of the NOTAM does not provide a regulatory defense

options.label: B
options.text: Partial violation — TFR incursions during active non-emergency TFRs (other than nuclear plant or disaster TFRs) are handled as administrative deviations; the pilot must file a pilot deviation report but receives no certificate action for a first TFR violation with no security consequence

options.label: C
options.text: No violation — the pilot conducted a thorough preflight check using the sectional chart; because Presidential TFRs are not depicted on sectional charts and the pilot had no reasonable method of knowing about the TFR, the FAA applies a good-faith safe harbor to TFR incursions caused by inadequate chart currency

options.label: D
options.text: Minor violation only — TFR violations that occur without intent and result in no incident are handled exclusively by NASA ASRS report filing; filing an ASRS report within 10 days provides complete immunity from FAA enforcement for any TFR incursion

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.103 requires pilots to 'become familiar with all available information concerning [a] flight,' specifically including NOTAMs. NOTAMs are the ONLY system that publishes TFRs — they are not and cannot be on sectional charts. A pilot who checks only the sectional for airspace restrictions has performed an incomplete preflight. The Presidential TFR violation (14 CFR 91.141) is serious: it typically triggers an immediate military intercept response, with the aircraft escorted to landing, and is followed by FAA enforcement. The FAA's position on TFR violations: 'I didn't check NOTAMs' is not a regulatory defense — it demonstrates non-compliance with 91.103. The 'thorough preflight is a defense' answer invents a 'good faith chart currency' defense that does not exist. The 'ASRS grants immunity' answer overstates the ASRS immunity — ASRS provides protection from civil penalty but not from certificate action, and does not cover willful violations. The 'administrative deviation tier' answer invents an 'administrative deviation' tier that does not apply to TFR violations, especially Presidential TFRs.

questions.text: A student pilot holds a valid student certificate and wishes to conduct a solo cross-country flight that will pass through the Washington D.C. 30 NM SFRA. Which of the following is required before the flight departs under 14 CFR 93.335?

options.label: A
options.text: The student must request a Letter of Authorization (LOA) from the DCA TRACON at least 5 business days prior to the planned flight; standard SFRA procedures are insufficient for solo student operations in the SFRA due to reduced situational awareness requirements

options.label: B
options.text: Student pilots are permanently prohibited from conducting solo operations within the 30 NM SFRA regardless of training or authorization; the SFRA requires a private certificate minimum due to the security sensitivity of the airspace and the aircraft intercept protocols in use

options.label: C
options.text: The student must complete the SFRA online training course, obtain a VFR flight plan, receive a discrete transponder code from ATC prior to departure, and maintain two-way radio communication throughout the SFRA transit; all SFRA requirements apply equally to student and private pilots

options.label: D
options.text: No additional requirements — student pilots are exempt from SFRA requirements because they are operating under CFI supervision even when on solo; the solo endorsement from a CFI constitutes adequate authorization for SFRA transit

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 93.335 and associated SFRA regulations apply to ALL aircraft and ALL pilots operating within the 30 NM SFRA, without exception for certificate type. The requirements for VFR flight in the SFRA are identical for student and private pilots: (1) Complete the FAA Safety Team SFRA online training course (free, at faasafety.gov). (2) File a VFR flight plan. (3) Obtain a discrete transponder code from ATC before departure. (4) Maintain two-way radio communication at all times in the SFRA. Student pilots with appropriate solo endorsements and SFRA training may legally operate in the SFRA. The SFRA does not require an LOA beyond these standard procedures for VFR operations. Note: the inner 15 NM FRZ has additional restrictions and requires specific security clearances for most civil operations. The 'CFI supervision exemption' answer invents a CFI supervision exemption for solo students. The '5-day LOA requirement' answer invents a 5-day LOA requirement. The 'permanently prohibited' answer incorrectly prohibits all student solo flight within the SFRA — the requirement is training and procedure compliance, not certificate level.

questions.text: On preflight NOTAM review, a pilot notes that Restricted Area R-2910A is listed as 'ACTIVE 1400Z-2200Z MON-FRI SFC-FL200.' The planned departure is Tuesday at 1630Z and the route passes through R-2910A at 9,500 feet MSL. What is the correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed and squawk 7700 while transiting R-2910A — Emergency transponder codes provide military controlling agencies with a visual alert that the VFR aircraft is aware of the Restricted Area; this constitutes adequate prior notification under 14 CFR 91.133

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed as planned — NOTAMs are advisory only for VFR aircraft; Restricted Areas require filing a NOTAM-based TFR waiver only for commercial Part 121/135 operations; VFR Part 91 pilots may transit Restricted Areas at their own risk without prior coordination

options.label: C
options.text: Contact enroute Center and request an IFR clearance through R-2910A — IFR aircraft may transit Restricted Areas during activity without coordination because ATC's IFR routing handles all conflict deconfliction with military operations automatically

options.label: D
options.text: Contact the controlling authority before departure to request authorization to transit R-2910A during the active window; if authorization is granted, the pilot may transit; if denied or unavailable, the pilot must route around the Restricted Area

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.133 prohibits civil aircraft from operating in Restricted Areas without authorization from the using or controlling agency. R-2910A is ACTIVE during the planned transit — 1630Z falls within the 1400-2200Z Monday-Friday active window. The correct procedure: contact the controlling authority (found in the Chart Supplement for R-2910A) and request authorization to transit at 9,500 feet MSL. If the authority grants a clearance window, the pilot may transit. If authorization is unavailable or denied, the pilot must route around. VFR status does not waive Restricted Area restrictions — NOTAMs for Restricted Area activation are legally binding on all aircraft. The 'ATC handles Restricted Areas automatically' answer incorrectly suggests ATC automatically handles Restricted Area coordination for IFR aircraft — ATC must still coordinate with the controlling military authority. The 'NOTAMs are advisory for VFR' answer falsely designates NOTAMs as advisory for VFR pilots. The '7700 notification' answer invents a 7700 'notification' procedure for Restricted Area transit that has no regulatory basis and would trigger unnecessary emergency response.

questions.text: During preflight planning, a pilot identifies a MOA along the route at cruise altitude. The Chart Supplement shows the controlling frequency as '128.9 Eglin Radar.' How should the pilot determine whether the MOA will be active during the planned transit?

options.label: A
options.text: Contact the controlling agency at 128.9 Eglin Radar or call the scheduling office phone number listed in the Chart Supplement to ask whether the MOA will be active during the planned transit time; if inactive, transit is legal and practically safe; if active, evaluate whether to reroute

options.label: B
options.text: Check the ATIS for the nearest Class C airport — if the ATIS does not mention the MOA as active, it is legally considered inactive for the duration of that ATIS broadcast cycle (typically 1 hour), and the pilot may transit without further coordination

options.label: C
options.text: File an IFR flight plan for the MOA transit portion — IFR aircraft have unlimited access to all MOAs regardless of activity status; once on an IFR flight plan, the pilot may proceed through the MOA without contacting the controlling authority

options.label: D
options.text: Assume the MOA is inactive — MOAs are activated only for planned military exercises that are NOTAM'd at least 48 hours in advance; the absence of a MOA activation NOTAM in the preflight briefing means the MOA is guaranteed to be inactive during the transit

questions.explanation: The Chart Supplement is the authoritative source for MOA controlling agency contact information. The practical procedure: (1) Find the MOA entry in the Chart Supplement — it lists floor, ceiling, time of use, and the controlling agency frequency and/or phone number. (2) Contact the controlling agency directly — either the scheduling office by phone before departure or the radar frequency (128.9 Eglin Radar) when airborne. For planned cross-countries, the preflight phone call is best. The controlling agency will confirm hot or cold status for the specific time window. If hot: evaluate rerouting around the MOA. If cold: transit is both legal and safe. The 'Class C ATIS verification' answer invents a Class C ATIS-based verification standard that does not exist. The 'IFR grants unlimited MOA access' answer falsely claims IFR aircraft have unlimited MOA access — ATC will not route IFR through an active MOA without coordination. The 'MOAs are always published in advance' answer falsely claims MOAs are always NOTAM'd in advance — many military MOAs can be activated on short notice without a published NOTAM.

questions.text: A wildfire has broken out in a mountainous area along a pilot's cross-country route. The pilot sees smoke and notes fire trucks on the ground. The pilot decides to circle the fire to observe it from 1,500 feet AGL. What SUA regulation is most likely applicable?

options.label: A
options.text: 14 CFR 91.159 — cruising altitude rules prohibit descending below 3,500 feet MSL on any heading between 180 and 359 degrees while in a circling maneuver; circling at 1,500 AGL violates VFR cruising altitude requirements regardless of fire emergency status

options.label: B
options.text: No regulation applies — wildfires on the ground are not aviation hazards; a pilot may circle any ground-based emergency at any altitude providing terrain clearance is maintained and no ATC facility has issued a NOTAM

options.label: C
options.text: 14 CFR 91.137 — a Temporary Flight Restriction may have been established around the wildfire protecting firefighting operations; civil aircraft may not fly below 2,000 feet AGL within a defined radius of the incident; the pilot must check for NOTAM TFRs before approaching a wildfire

options.label: D
options.text: 14 CFR 91.119 — minimum safe altitude rules prohibit flight over any emergency site below 1,000 feet AGL in non-congested areas; the 1,500 AGL flight is legal but the pilot should ascend to 2,500 AGL for a larger safety margin

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.137 authorizes the FAA to issue Temporary Flight Restrictions around disaster or emergency areas including wildfires to protect firefighting operations and emergency personnel. When a TFR is established under 91.137, civil aircraft may not operate within the TFR boundary below 2,000 feet AGL unless specifically authorized. Firefighting aircraft/tankers are making low-altitude passes; civilian sightseers seriously jeopardize these operations. Several fatal accidents and near-misses have involved civilian aircraft and aerial firefighting tankers in active fire TFRs. The pilot circling a wildfire at 1,500 AGL may be violating an active TFR published while the pilot was airborne. The correct action: check NOTAMs for TFR coverage before approaching. The 'no regulation applies' answer falsely claims no regulation applies. The '91.119 minimum-altitude' answer identifies a real regulation (91.119) but it doesn't specifically address firefighting TFRs. The '91.159 cruising-altitude' answer misapplies the cruising altitude rule (91.159 applies to level VFR cruise, not orbiting maneuvers).

questions.text: A pilot checks weather and files a VFR flight plan, but does not complete a NOTAM briefing because 'I fly this route every week and nothing is ever there.' Halfway through the flight, the pilot's EFB sends a pop-up TFR alert showing an active 10 NM Presidential TFR directly ahead — the President is visiting a nearby city. The TFR base is the surface. What is the SAFEST immediate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue through the TFR at maximum altitude — flying at the highest altitude possible within the TFR keeps the aircraft above the high-risk intercept zone near 3,000 AGL; POTUS TFRs only affect low-altitude aircraft below 3,000 AGL

options.label: B
options.text: Proceed and land at the nearest airport inside the TFR — landing immediately puts the aircraft on the ground which ends the TFR violation and removes intercept risk; ATC cannot intercept a parked aircraft and the pilot can explain the situation from the ground

options.label: C
options.text: Declare an emergency on 121.5 — entering a Presidential TFR boundary constitutes an in-flight emergency that requires immediate ATC clearance to transit; declaring emergency allows medical and security personnel to authorize the transit under 14 CFR 91.3 emergency provisions

options.label: D
options.text: Immediately turn away from the TFR boundary to remain clear, contact ATC on the current frequency to report the situation and request vectors away from the TFR, squawk the assigned discrete code or 1200, and deviate from the TFR route; if not in contact with ATC, contact the nearest facility immediately

questions.explanation: The safest and most legally correct action upon recognizing an imminent TFR conflict is immediate deviation and ATC contact. The sequence: (1) Turn away from the TFR boundary immediately — do not continue toward it hoping to get authorization mid-flight. (2) Contact ATC on the current frequency and advise of the situation: 'We have a TFR conflict ahead — requesting vectors clear of the TFR.' (3) Squawk the assigned code or 1200 and maintain TWC with ATC. ATC can provide vectors, confirm the TFR boundaries, and coordinate if needed. The goal is to demonstrate positive compliance intent before the boundary is crossed — if a military intercept is triggered, a pilot who has already turned and contacted ATC faces a significantly more favorable enforcement outcome than one who continued. The 'continue at maximum altitude' answer is Invulnerability — rationalizing altitude as a defense against intercept. Presidential TFRs extend from the surface to FL600. The 'declare an emergency' answer over-escalates — a TFR conflict en route is not in itself an emergency; deviation and ATC contact are the correct response. The 'land inside the TFR' answer is Macho — intentionally entering the TFR to land inside it is still a violation and compounds the risk.
questions.sjt_rationale: The precipitating error is complacency in NOTAM review ('I fly this route every week'). The immediate decision is the test: deviation and ATC contact vs. continuation or escalation. Turning away and contacting ATC demonstrates situation awareness, positive corrective action, and regulatory compliance intent.

questions.text: During a checkride oral, the DPE presents a sectional with blue-hatched airspace and says: 'You are VFR at 6,000 feet. This is your position — you are about to enter this airspace. It is currently active. What do you do?' The applicant says: 'Oh, that's a MOA — I'm legal to go through it VFR.' Upon closer inspection, the DPE reveals the label reads 'R-2910.' What error did the applicant make, and what is the correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: Minor error — Restricted Areas and MOAs have the same VFR entry requirements under 14 CFR 91.133; the applicant's practical decision (proceed VFR) is correct even though the designation terminology is wrong; DPE should give partial credit for the correct operational outcome

options.label: B
options.text: Critical error — R-2910 is a Restricted Area, not an MOA; 14 CFR 91.133 prohibits civil aircraft from operating in active Restricted Areas without authorization from the controlling agency; the VFR entry exception applies to MOAs, not Restricted Areas; the correct action is to turn away immediately and contact ATC or the controlling agency to request authorization

options.label: C
options.text: No error — R-prefix airspace is still classified as MOA-equivalent for VFR purposes; the 'R' designation indicates Restricted only for IFR traffic; the applicant's analysis is correct and the transit is legal for VFR operations

options.label: D
options.text: The applicant was correct until the label clarification — MOA and Restricted Area differ only in controlling authority; once the controlling authority (military vs. FAA) is confirmed, the VFR entry rule is the same: legal for VFR without clearance during business hours

questions.explanation: The applicant made a critical SUA identification error: confusing a Restricted Area (R-prefix, blue hatching) with an MOA (magenta hatching, different label format). The distinction has direct operational consequences: MOAs: VFR entry is legal at any time without ATC authorization. Restricted Areas: civil aircraft entry requires authorization from the controlling agency when active — VFR or IFR. An 'R-2910 ACTIVE' designation means the pilot cannot enter without authorization under 14 CFR 91.133. The applicant's blue-hatching visual misidentification as an MOA would lead directly to an unauthorized Restricted Area entry — which can trigger military intercept and enforcement action. The correct response: turn away, contact ATC or the controlling authority, request authorization, and wait for authorization before transiting. The 'R equals a MOA for VFR' answer invents an 'R = MOA equivalent for VFR' interpretation that has no legal basis. The 'MOA and Restricted Area rules match' answer falsely equates MOA and Restricted Area entry rules. The 'business-hours inactive' answer invents a 'business hours' automatic inactive status for Restricted Areas.
questions.sjt_rationale: Sectional chart literacy is a prerequisite for safe SUA operations. The test is whether the applicant can identify airspace class from visual symbols before reasoning about entry rules. Confusing R-prefix (Restricted) with MOA (magenta label) is the most dangerous chart-reading error in SUA operations.
